questions.title: AWS Regions, Availability Zones and Global Infrastructure
questions.question: What are AWS Regions and Availability Zones and why do they matter for backend architecture?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Region: geographic area with multiple AZs (e.g., us-east-1, ap-south-1)
- Availability Zone: one or more isolated data centers within a region, separate power/networking
- High availability: deploy across multiple AZs — failure of one AZ doesn't bring down the service
- Latency: choose a region close to your users to minimize network round trips
- Data residency: some regulations require data to stay in specific regions (GDPR → EU regions)
- Services that are regional: EC2, RDS, ECS; global services: IAM, CloudFront, Route53

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A Region is a geographic location — like Mumbai (ap-south-1) or Virginia (us-east-1) — that contains multiple Availability Zones. An Availability Zone is essentially one or more physically separate data centers within the region, with independent power, cooling, and networking. The physical separation means a failure in one AZ — a power outage, flood, or hardware failure — doesn't affect the others.

For backend architecture, AZs are the foundation of high availability. You deploy your application in at least two AZs behind a load balancer. If one AZ has a problem, the load balancer routes all traffic to instances in the healthy AZ. Your database runs in Multi-AZ mode, where the standby is in a different AZ and automatic failover happens in minutes.

Region choice matters for latency and compliance. If your users are in India, running in ap-south-1 Mumbai gives 10-20ms latency versus 200ms from us-east-1. If you're handling EU user data, GDPR may require you to run in eu-west or eu-central regions.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## AWS Global Structure

```
AWS Cloud
├── Region: us-east-1 (N. Virginia)
│   ├── AZ: us-east-1a (Data Center Cluster A)
│   ├── AZ: us-east-1b (Data Center Cluster B)
│   └── AZ: us-east-1c (Data Center Cluster C)
├── Region: ap-south-1 (Mumbai)
│   ├── AZ: ap-south-1a
│   ├── AZ: ap-south-1b
│   └── AZ: ap-south-1c
└── Region: eu-west-1 (Ireland)
    ├── AZ: eu-west-1a
    └── ...
```

## Multi-AZ Architecture (Java Backend)

```
                    Internet
                       │
               [Route 53 DNS]
                       │
            [Application Load Balancer]
                 /            \
    AZ-1a                         AZ-1b
    [EC2/ECS App Server]    [EC2/ECS App Server]
           │                        │
    [RDS Primary]  ←──────→  [RDS Standby]
    (AZ-1a)        sync repl   (AZ-1b)
```

## Key Regional vs Global Services

| Service | Scope |
|---------|-------|
| EC2, ECS, RDS | Regional (choose AZ) |
| S3 | Regional (globally accessible) |
| IAM | Global |
| Route 53 | Global |
| CloudFront | Global (edge locations) |
| VPC | Regional |

## Spring Boot: Configuring AWS SDK Region

```java
@Configuration
public class AwsConfig {
    @Value("${aws.region:ap-south-1}")
    private String region;

    @Bean
    public S3Client s3Client() {
        return S3Client.builder()
            .region(Region.of(region))
            .credentialsProvider(DefaultCredentialsProvider.create())
            .build();
    }
}
```

speakable_v2.hook: A Region is a geographic location — like Mumbai (ap-south-1) or Virginia (us-east-1) — that contains multiple Availability Zones.
speakable_v2.cap: If you're handling EU user data, GDPR may require you to run in eu-west or eu-central regions.

questions.title: VPC, Subnets and Security Groups
questions.question: How does AWS VPC networking work and how do you secure a Java backend with subnets and security groups?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- VPC: isolated virtual network with your own IP address range (CIDR block)
- Public subnet: has route to Internet Gateway — for load balancers, NAT gateways
- Private subnet: no direct internet route — for application servers and databases
- Security Group: stateful firewall rules at the instance level — allow inbound/outbound traffic
- NACL: stateless subnet-level firewall — less common, but provides subnet-level isolation
- NAT Gateway: lets private subnet instances initiate outbound internet traffic (for package downloads, API calls)
- Principle: database in private subnet, only accessible from app security group

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A VPC is your private isolated network within AWS. You define a CIDR block — the range of IP addresses — and divide it into subnets. Public subnets have a route to the Internet Gateway and are for resources that need to be directly accessible from the internet, like your load balancer. Private subnets have no direct internet route and are for your application servers and databases.

The recommended Java backend architecture is to put your load balancer in the public subnet, your application servers in a private subnet, and your database in a separate private subnet. The application servers can reach the internet for outbound calls through a NAT Gateway in the public subnet, but no inbound traffic from the internet can reach them directly.

Security Groups act as stateful firewalls per resource. Stateful means if you allow inbound traffic on port 8080, the response traffic is automatically allowed without a separate outbound rule. A best practice is chaining security groups — the database security group only allows inbound on port 5432 from the application security group's ID, not from a CIDR range. This means only your actual app instances can talk to the database.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Recommended VPC Layout

```
VPC: 10.0.0.0/16
├── Public Subnet AZ-a: 10.0.1.0/24
│   ├── Application Load Balancer
│   └── NAT Gateway
├── Public Subnet AZ-b: 10.0.2.0/24
│   └── Application Load Balancer (multi-AZ)
├── Private Subnet AZ-a: 10.0.10.0/24
│   └── ECS/EC2 App Servers
├── Private Subnet AZ-b: 10.0.11.0/24
│   └── ECS/EC2 App Servers
├── DB Subnet AZ-a: 10.0.20.0/24
│   └── RDS Primary
└── DB Subnet AZ-b: 10.0.21.0/24
    └── RDS Standby
```

## Security Group Chain

```
ALB Security Group:
  Inbound: 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (internet)
  Outbound: 8080 to App-SG

App Security Group:
  Inbound: 8080 from ALB-SG only
  Outbound: 5432 to DB-SG, 443 to 0.0.0.0/0 (via NAT)

DB Security Group:
  Inbound: 5432 from App-SG only  ← only app can reach DB
  Outbound: (not needed for RDS)
```

## Spring Boot: Use IAM Roles, Not Hardcoded Credentials

```yaml
# application.yml — no AWS keys here!
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://${RDS_ENDPOINT}:5432/appdb
    # RDS_ENDPOINT injected via environment variable or Secrets Manager
```

```java
// AWS SDK automatically uses EC2/ECS instance role credentials
// No access keys needed when running on AWS with proper IAM role
S3Client s3 = S3Client.builder()
    .credentialsProvider(DefaultCredentialsProvider.create())
    // DefaultCredentialsProvider checks: env vars → system props → EC2 instance metadata
    .build();
```

speakable_v2.hook: A VPC is your private isolated network within AWS.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This means only your actual app instances can talk to the database.

questions.title: EC2 Instance Types and Auto Scaling
questions.question: How do you choose EC2 instance types and set up auto scaling for a Java Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Instance families: t-series (burstable, cheap), m-series (general purpose), c-series (compute), r-series (memory)
- For Java apps: m5/m6i general purpose or c5/c6i for CPU-intensive workloads
- JVM needs memory: heap + metaspace + thread stacks — don't size EC2 just for heap
- Auto Scaling Group (ASG): automatically add/remove instances based on metrics
- Scaling policies: target tracking (maintain 60% CPU), step scaling, scheduled scaling
- Lifecycle hooks: run custom actions before instance terminates (graceful shutdown)
- Use launch templates, not launch configurations (newer, more features)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For a Java Spring Boot backend, I typically start with m-series instances — general purpose with a balanced CPU to memory ratio. Java applications need more memory than their configured heap because the JVM also uses memory for metaspace, thread stacks, and native libraries. A rule of thumb is to provision 2-3x your max heap size as total instance memory. So if you configure -Xmx2g, use an instance with at least 4-6GB RAM.

T-series burstable instances are cheaper but unreliable for consistent workloads. They earn CPU credits when idle and spend them during bursts. A Java backend that has steady consistent load will run out of CPU credits and be throttled, causing unpredictable latency spikes. Use t-series only for dev/test environments.

Auto Scaling Groups are how you handle variable load. You define minimum, desired, and maximum instance counts, and policies that trigger scaling. Target tracking is the simplest — tell it to keep average CPU at 60% and it adds or removes instances automatically. For Spring Boot, add a lifecycle hook to give instances 30-60 seconds to finish in-flight requests before termination.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Instance Type Selection

| Family | Best For | Java Use Case |
|--------|----------|---------------|
| t3/t4g | Dev/Test, low traffic | Non-production only |
| m5/m6i | General purpose | Standard Spring Boot apps |
| c5/c6i | Compute-intensive | High-throughput APIs, batch |
| r5/r6i | Memory-intensive | Large heap JVM, Elasticsearch |
| g4/g5 | GPU | ML inference |

## JVM Memory Sizing

```
EC2 Memory: 8GB
├── JVM Heap (-Xmx):    4GB
├── Metaspace:         512MB
├── Thread stacks:     256MB (100 threads × 256KB)
├── DirectByteBuffer:  512MB (Netty, NIO)
├── OS overhead:      ~1GB
└── Free buffer:      ~768MB

JVM flags for 8GB instance:
-Xms2g -Xmx4g -XX:MetaspaceSize=256m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m
```

## Auto Scaling with Graceful Shutdown

```java
// Spring Boot: graceful shutdown (built-in since 2.3)
// application.yml
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s  # wait up to 30s for in-flight requests
```

```bash
# ASG Lifecycle Hook — give container 60s to drain
# In User Data or lifecycle hook action:
aws autoscaling complete-lifecycle-action \
  --lifecycle-action-result CONTINUE \
  --lifecycle-hook-name app-termination-hook \
  --auto-scaling-group-name my-asg \
  --instance-id $INSTANCE_ID
```

## CloudWatch Scaling Policy

```json
{
  "PolicyType": "TargetTrackingScaling",
  "TargetTrackingConfiguration": {
    "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {
      "PredefinedMetricType": "ASGAverageCPUUtilization"
    },
    "TargetValue": 60.0,
    "ScaleInCooldown": 300,
    "ScaleOutCooldown": 60
  }
}
```

speakable_v2.hook: For a Java Spring Boot backend, I typically start with m-series instances — general purpose with a balanced CPU to memory ratio.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: For Spring Boot, add a lifecycle hook to give instances 30-60 seconds to finish in-flight requests before termination.

questions.title: AWS Load Balancers — ALB vs NLB
questions.question: What is the difference between ALB and NLB in AWS and when do you use each for a Java backend?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- ALB (Application Load Balancer): Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) — routes by path, host, headers; supports WebSocket, gRPC
- NLB (Network Load Balancer): Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) — ultra-low latency, preserves source IP, handles millions of connections
- ALB target types: EC2 instances, ECS tasks, Lambda, IP addresses
- Path-based routing: /api/* → backend service, /static/* → S3 or frontend service
- ALB sticky sessions: route same client to same backend (use with caution)
- Health checks: ALB checks HTTP endpoint; NLB checks TCP connection
- NLB: use for gaming, IoT, financial trading — when latency matters more than HTTP features

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For most Java Spring Boot backends, the Application Load Balancer is the right choice. It operates at HTTP level, so you can make routing decisions based on URL paths, host headers, or HTTP headers. This enables you to put multiple microservices behind one ALB and route based on path — /api/orders routes to the order service, /api/inventory routes to the inventory service.

ALB also integrates natively with AWS Certificate Manager for HTTPS termination, with Cognito for authentication, and with WAF for security rules. The backend receives plain HTTP, which reduces the complexity in your Spring Boot application.

NLB is for when you need extreme low latency or need to preserve the client's source IP. It operates at TCP level and doesn't parse HTTP at all — packets are just forwarded. You'd use NLB for WebSocket connections that need very high throughput, or for non-HTTP protocols. A common pattern is NLB in front of ALB when you need a static IP address, since ALB doesn't have static IPs but NLB does.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## ALB Path-Based Routing

```
ALB: api.example.com
├── /api/orders/*    → Target Group: order-service (ECS tasks)
├── /api/products/*  → Target Group: product-service (ECS tasks)
├── /api/auth/*      → Target Group: auth-service (ECS tasks)
└── /* (default)     → Target Group: frontend (EC2 or S3 redirect)
```

## ALB vs NLB Comparison

| Feature | ALB | NLB |
|---------|-----|-----|
| Layer | 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) | 4 (TCP/UDP) |
| Routing | Path, host, headers | IP+Port |
| Latency | ~1-5ms | <1ms |
| Static IP | No (DNS only) | Yes |
| SSL Termination | Yes | Yes (passthrough option) |
| WebSocket | Yes | Yes |
| gRPC | Yes | Yes |
| Source IP Preservation | Via X-Forwarded-For header | Native |

## Health Check Configuration

```
# Spring Boot Actuator health endpoint for ALB health checks
GET /actuator/health → 200 OK = healthy, 5xx = unhealthy
```

```yaml
# application.yml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      base-path: /actuator
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized

# ALB Health Check settings:
# Path: /actuator/health
# Interval: 30s
# Healthy threshold: 2 (consecutive 200s)
# Unhealthy threshold: 3 (consecutive failures)
# Timeout: 5s
```

## Spring Boot: Get Client IP Behind ALB

```java
@GetMapping("/api/info")
public String getClientInfo(HttpServletRequest request) {
    // ALB adds X-Forwarded-For with original client IP
    String clientIp = request.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For");
    if (clientIp == null) clientIp = request.getRemoteAddr();
    return clientIp;
}
```

speakable_v2.hook: For most Java Spring Boot backends, the Application Load Balancer is the right choice.
speakable_v2.cap: A common pattern is NLB in front of ALB when you need a static IP address, since ALB doesn't have static IPs but NLB does.

questions.title: Monitoring with CloudWatch
questions.question: How do you set up effective monitoring and alerting for a Java Spring Boot application using CloudWatch?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- CloudWatch Metrics: time-series data — EC2 CPU, memory (with CloudWatch agent), custom app metrics
- CloudWatch Logs: centralized log aggregation from EC2/ECS — filter and alarm on log patterns
- CloudWatch Alarms: trigger SNS notifications or Auto Scaling actions based on metric thresholds
- Metric filters: extract numeric values from log lines (error count, p99 latency)
- CloudWatch Container Insights: ECS/EKS container-level metrics
- Spring Boot Micrometer → CloudWatch metrics publisher
- Dashboard: combine multiple metrics for at-a-glance operational view

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring and observability service. For a Spring Boot application, I set up three layers of monitoring. First, infrastructure metrics — EC2 CPU, memory (requires the CloudWatch agent), network, and disk. Second, application metrics via Micrometer, which is Spring Boot's metrics facade. Third, log monitoring via CloudWatch Logs where I create metric filters to count errors and trigger alarms.

Micrometer with the CloudWatch metrics registry lets you publish custom application metrics — JVM heap usage, database connection pool utilization, custom business metrics like orders per minute — directly to CloudWatch. You then build dashboards combining infrastructure and application metrics for a complete operational view.

For alerting, I set CloudWatch Alarms on the most actionable metrics. CPU alarm for scaling, 5xx error rate alarm for application problems, database connection exhaustion alarm for capacity issues. Alarms trigger SNS notifications which can email the team, trigger a PagerDuty incident, or send a Slack message.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring and observability service.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Alarms trigger SNS notifications which can email the team, trigger a PagerDuty incident, or send a Slack message.

questions.title: AWS Secrets Manager and Parameter Store
questions.question: How do you securely manage database credentials and API keys in a Spring Boot application on AWS?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Never hardcode credentials in code or application.yml committed to git
- AWS Secrets Manager: stores and rotates secrets (DB passwords, API keys) — costs per secret
- AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: free tier available, SSM GetParameter in code
- Secrets Manager rotation: automatic credential rotation with Lambda — no restart needed
- Spring Cloud AWS: Spring-native integration for reading Secrets Manager and Parameter Store
- IAM role on EC2/ECS: grants application permission to read specific secrets only
- At rest encryption: Secrets Manager uses KMS by default

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The fundamental rule is that credentials should never appear in source code or in configuration files that get committed to a repository. AWS provides two services for this: Secrets Manager for sensitive secrets that need rotation like database passwords, and Parameter Store for configuration values and less sensitive parameters.

Secrets Manager is the better choice for database credentials because it integrates with RDS to automatically rotate passwords on a schedule. When a rotation happens, Secrets Manager updates the secret value and you read the latest value from the SDK — your application doesn't need to restart. This is hugely valuable for security because you can rotate credentials regularly without any downtime.

For Spring Boot, Spring Cloud AWS provides a bootstrap integration that reads from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store at startup and makes the values available as Spring properties. Your application.yml references ${db.password} and Spring resolves it from the secret store. The application gets the IAM permission to read those specific secrets through its EC2 or ECS task role — no access keys needed.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: The fundamental rule is that credentials should never appear in source code or in configuration files that get committed to a repository.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: The application gets the IAM permission to read those specific secrets through its EC2 or ECS task role — no access keys needed.

questions.title: AWS SQS and SNS for Async Communication
questions.question: How do you use AWS SQS and SNS for asynchronous messaging in a Java Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- SQS: message queue — point-to-point, messages stored until consumed, auto-retry
- SNS: pub/sub topic — one publisher, many subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email)
- Standard queue: at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering
- FIFO queue: exactly-once processing, strict ordering, lower throughput
- Dead Letter Queue (DLQ): messages that fail after max retries go here for investigation
- Visibility timeout: message hidden from other consumers while being processed
- Fan-out pattern: SNS topic → multiple SQS queues for different services

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
SQS is a message queue for point-to-point async communication. One producer sends a message, one consumer picks it up, processes it, and deletes it. If processing fails, the message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and another consumer can pick it up and retry. After too many failures, it goes to the Dead Letter Queue for investigation. This pattern decouples services and provides natural buffering against load spikes.

SNS is a pub/sub system. You publish one message to a topic and SNS fan-outs to all subscribers — SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email. This is how you implement the fan-out pattern: an order placed event publishes to an SNS topic, and the inventory service, notification service, and analytics service each have their own SQS queue subscribed to that topic.

For Spring Boot, Spring Cloud AWS provides @SqsListener annotations that work similarly to @KafkaListener — you annotate a method and the framework handles polling, message parsing, and deletion on successful processing.
